\title{Measuring Complex Tastes: A Multiple Factor Analysis of Preferences, Consumption, and Evaluations in Musical Taste}

\author{Omar Lizardo\\ \small University of California, Los Angeles} \date{October 2026}

\begin{document}

\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
\noindent This paper develops a way to measure complex tastes---cases where what people like, do, and praise do not line up---using data that record preferences, engagement, and evaluations of the same objects, whether genre categories or specific cultural items. The approach applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA), a Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) method, and lets us ask concrete questions about complex tastes: Do preference, engagement, and evaluation contribute equally to the structure that emerges? Do some dimensions of complex taste hang together more than others? The method also captures a duality: individuals vary in how much their own tastes are complex, and genres vary in how much they attract complex tastes from the people who encounter them. I demonstrate the approach using data on Americans' tastes in twenty musical genres, collected around 2012.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

Sociologists have measured cultural taste in at least three different ways \citep{ma2026tastes}. One tradition treats taste as \emph{preference}: a person's affective response to a cultural object. A second treats it as an orientation toward \emph{consumption}: actual participation or engagement in a cultural field. A third treats it as a faculty expressed in \emph{valuation}: judgments about the quality or status of cultural objects. Rather than resolving this ambiguity by fiat, \citet{ma2026tastes} argues that taste should be understood pluralistically, as a person's ``thick subjectivity'' in a cultural field---a multidimensional orientation expressed through the multiple aspects of action that guide our preferences, engagement, and evaluations.

Taking taste's multiple aspects seriously sharpens the idea of \emph{complex taste}. In simple tastes, the aspects agree: what a person likes, does, and values all point the same way. In complex tastes they do not: the guilty pleasure (liked and consumed but not valued), the taste pose (liked and valued but not consumed), distanced consumption (consumed but neither liked nor valued), and their kin \citep{ma2026tastes}.

This paper takes that pluralist conception seriously and builds a measurement strategy to match. The strategy applies Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}---a member of the Geometric Data Analysis (GDA) family that \citet{bourdieu1984distinction} used in his classic study \citep{rouanet2000geometric-a44, roux2004geometric-65c}---to a data structure in which each cultural object is described by three sets of indicators, one per each aspect of complex taste. MFA's block structure lets us ask the questions the theory of complex tastes raises directly, such as how strong are the links between preference, consumption, and evaluation? Do the three aspects contribute equally to the shared structure of taste? And what does the geometric signature of independent taste aspects look like when mapped to the same shared space?

\section{Data and Measures}

\subsection{Data Source}

This analysis uses the Survey Sample International (SSI) 2012 Cultural Tastes Survey \citep{lizardo2012ssi},\footnote{The survey data and documentation are publicly available at \url{https://olizardo.github.io/SSI-2012/}.} a nationally representative sample of $N = 2{,}276$ U.S. adults surveyed in 2012. The survey asked respondents about their relationship to twenty musical genres, capturing how they feel about each genre, whether they engage with it, and how they perceive the people who enjoy it. After removing the 17 respondents with incomplete data on any of the 60 analysis variables, the working sample contains $N = 2{,}259$ respondents.

\subsection{Operationalizing the Three Aspects of Taste}

To measure complex tastes, we need distinct measures of preference, consumption, and evaluation for each genre. The survey collects data on all three, though operationalizing them as comparable binary indicators requires careful choices.

We operationalize preference as affective response by recoding the four-point liking scale (like, dislike, neither, or not familiar) into a binary: $1$ if the respondent likes the genre, $0$ otherwise. This treatment includes unfamiliar genres as non-preference, resting on the reasoning that genuine affective preference requires at least knowing the object. You cannot prefer a genre you've never heard of. Consumption, by contrast, is straightforward. The survey asked respondents whether they had listened to each genre in the past month, a direct behavioral indicator coded $1$ for yes and $0$ for no. This gives us a clear measure of engagement independent of what people report liking. 

Evaluation poses the most difficult measurement challenge. To assess how respondents perceive the social status of each genre's fans, the survey asked them to mark a check-all-that-apply list of characteristics: college-educated, middle-class, upper-class, working-class, lower-class, and so on. But respondents often mark contradictory pairs, checking both ``college-educated'' and ``not college-educated,'' or both ``middle-class'' and ``upper-class''---a pattern that reflects genuine social ambiguity in how audiences are perceived. Yet for our analysis we need a single binary measure of high status attribution. We solve this by deeming a respondent to have high evaluation of a genre only when they signal \emph{unambiguous} high status. Specifically, a genre receives a $1$ if the respondent either checked college-educated \emph{without} checking not college-educated, \emph{or} checked middle or upper class \emph{without} checking working or lower class. This conservative standard requires respondents to avoid contradicting themselves, which makes evaluation the rarest of the three signals, as respondents attribute unambiguous high status to fewer genres than they like or listen to.

Table~\ref{tab:genre-rates} shows the prevalence of each coding. Overall, $41.7\%$ of genre-responses are coded $1$ on preference, $22.9\%$ on consumption, and $20.7\%$ on evaluation. The step down from preference to evaluation is striking: respondents like more genres than they listen to, and listen to more than they credit with high status. The unambiguous-status standard is demanding, requiring clear social positioning without internal contradiction, so evaluation becomes the least frequently affirmed aspect of taste.

\section{Results: Mapping the Space of Complex Tastes}

As we have seen, our data gives us three separate pictures of each person's taste: what they like, what they listen to, and what they think about the people who do. These three pictures might overlap heavily (a person who likes opera probably listens to it and sees its fans as high status), or they might diverge sharply (someone might listen to hip-hop while considering it low status and claiming not to like it). To answer our core questions---how much do these three pictures agree, do they contribute equally to a single coherent picture, and where do people end up when their pictures don't line up---we use Multiple Factor Analysis (MFA) \citep{pages2014mfa,abdi2013mfa}. This method takes data organized into distinct blocks of variables (here, the three aspects of taste) and builds a single shared picture of respondents while ensuring no one block dominates. We use \emph{blocks of variables}, or \emph{aspects} when referring specifically to preference, engagement, and evaluation, reserving ``group'' for its ordinary sociological meaning.

\subsection{The Global Structure of Taste: Constructing the Compromise Space}
\label{sec:mfa}

The raw data is a table with one row per respondent and sixty columns: twenty genres, each measured on three aspects. Each entry is binary, containing a 1 if the person likes/listens to/evaluates the genre highly, and 0 otherwise. To construct the global space combining preferences, consumption, and evaluations, we proceed in two steps. 

In the first step, we run a separate analysis on just the liking data (20 genres, 2,259 respondents), treating it as a two-way table of yes/no responses. This analysis shows how respondents cluster by what they like. We repeat the process independently for listening and for evaluations. In GDA terms, each of these is a Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) on one block of twenty binary variables and the same number of individuals. MCA is a method designed for categorical data that positions respondents and categories in a shared space according to their yes/no patterns, in much the way that standard correlations or principal components work for continuous data \citep{roux2004geometric-65c}. The result of each separate MCA is a map of the respondents, showing who is similar to whom in terms of liking alone, listening alone, or evaluations alone.

After the first step, the next step is to merge these three separate pictures into one. But we face a problem here because if one aspect naturally has stronger patterns than another (if listening, say, reveals much sharper clustering than evaluations), it will dominate the combined picture. To prevent this, we weight each aspect inversely to the magnitude of the eigenvalue corresponding to the first dimension of the separate MCA we just described \citep{pages2014mfa}. The first dimension of the MCA for preference had an eigenvalue of $0.155$; for consumption, $0.127$; for evaluation, $0.194$. The aspect with the largest eigenvalue ($\lambda_1$) has the strongest patterns, so we downweight it by using the weight $1/\lambda_1$. That gives weights of $6.45$ for preference ($1/0.155$), $7.90$ for consumption ($1/0.127$), and $5.15$ for evaluation ($1/0.194$). 

We apply these weights by multiplying each column in each aspect block by its corresponding weight and standardizing the resulting values by centering them around their mean. This weighting transformation converts the binary yes/no variables into continuous numerical values that reflect the relative strength of patterns within each aspect. We then combine the three weighted blocks into a single data table and perform a principal components analysis (PCA) on this combined weighted table, which simultaneously decomposes the respondent cloud into the shared compromise space and preserves the distinct structure of each aspect. The result is the ``complex taste space''---a single map of respondents where all three aspects are heard equally.\footnote{Respondents who give a constant answer within an aspect---liking all twenty genres or none, listening to all or none, granting unambiguous high status to the fans of all twenty genres or of none ($N = 412$, mostly the $321$ who grant status to no genre)---are treated as supplementary individuals, projected onto the space rather than contributing to its construction. They are excluded from the active subsample ($N = 1{,}847$) because constancy within a block is a nonresponse pattern, not a substantive taste position; respondents constant in one block typically vary in others. As a robustness check, we re-estimated the MFA treating them as active and the previous fit as supplementary; the substantive results are unchanged. We also re-estimated the same MFA with each block analyzed by scaled PCA instead of MCA; the results hold. Eigenvalues, RV coefficients, and individual coordinates correlate at $r > 0.96$ across the first four dimensions. The main difference is how rare categories are weighted: MCA emphasizes rare (distinctive) answers, a feature we want here since unusual taste patterns carry theoretical interest.}

\subsubsection{Are the Three Aspects Empirically Distinct?}

Before interpreting what the resulting dimensions reveal, we must establish whether the three aspects are genuinely separate measures or different angles on the same underlying structure. The RV coefficient, the multivariate analog of a correlation, answers this question. It measures how similarly two aspects rank respondents relative to each other by comparing their respondent-similarity matrices:

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{RV}(h,k) = \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_k)}{\sqrt{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h^2)\,\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_k^2)}}.
\label{eq:rv}
\end{equation}

Here, $\mathbf{S}_h$ is the respondent-similarity matrix for aspect $h$,\footnote{Formally, $\mathbf{S}_h = \mathbf{X}_h^\mathsf{T} \mathbf{X}_h$, where $\mathbf{X}_h$ is the $N \times J$ indicator matrix for aspect $h$ (centered and standardized according to MCA weighting: columns scaled by $(1-p_j)/\sqrt{p_j(1-p_j)}$ where $p_j$ is the column mass). Each entry $S_{h,ij}$ measures the weighted overlap in indicator choices between respondents $i$ and $j$ across all $J=20$ genre categories for that aspect.} capturing pairwise respondent similarities based on that aspect's twenty genres. RV ranges from 0 (complete independence: one aspect's pattern of who-is-similar-to-whom is entirely unrelated to the other aspect's pattern) to 1 (perfect alignment: the two aspects order all respondent pairs identically).

For preference and consumption, we find RV = 0.35---moderately similar but far from identical. Respondents who are similar in their liking patterns tend to be similar in their listening patterns, but the ranking of respondent pairs differs substantially between the two aspects. One respondent might be a heavy engager with moderate discriminating taste, while another is an intense discriminator who listens rarely.\footnote{We conducted all analyses in \textsf{R} using the \textsf{FactoMineR} package \citep{le2008factominer}; scripts reproducing all results are available at \url{https://github.com/olizardo/measuring-complex-tastes}.} Evaluation tells quite a different story. It shows an RV of $0.014$ with preference and $0.015$ with consumption---near-zero values that are the key empirical finding. Evaluations rank respondents almost completely independently of liking and listening. Knowing whether someone likes many genres tells you virtually nothing about whether they grant high status to those genres' fans. The three aspects of complex tastes are thus genuinely distinct empirically. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three partially separable dimensions of taste. This independence is why complex tastes can exist geometrically: a person can like a genre without listening to it, listen without liking, or evaluate highly without doing either.

\subsubsection{The Four Dimensions of Taste}

The global space resulting from the MFA analysis described in section~\ref{sec:mfa} organizes respondents along four interpretable dimensions, each capturing a distinct structure in how preferences, engagement, and evaluations align or diverge. Table~\ref{tab:eigen} shows that the first dimension captures $8.23\%$ of the variation, the second $7.25\%$, the third $5.39\%$, the fourth $5.11\%$, and the first five dimensions together $30.35\%$.\footnote{These percentages are typical for data like ours---binary yes/no responses scattered across twenty genres analyzed via MCA. Much of the variation is genre-specific (whether you like opera has little to do with whether you like hip-hop), so no single dimension captures huge amounts.} In the GDA tradition, this variation is called \emph{inertia}---the total spread or dispersion of the respondent cloud around its center. When we say a dimension captures $8.23\%$ of the inertia, we mean that ordering respondents along that dimension explains $8.23\%$ of how different they are from one another in their sixty-dimensional response pattern.

To understand what each dimension means, we examine where the twenty genres land in the space. For each genre and aspect, the MFA assigns a position along each dimension based on respondents' patterns; genres with many "yes" answers sit where respondents who gave those answers cluster, while genres with few "yes" answers sit where their rare endorsers sit. These positions, shown in Figure~\ref{fig:categories1-2} and~\ref{fig:categories3-4}, reveal the structure each dimension captures. 

On the first dimension, preference and consumption place genres cleanly along the traditional prestige hierarchy. The consecrated genres sit on the positive side (opera at $+0.72$ for consumption and $+0.61$ for preference; classical at $+0.64$ for consumption; big band at $+0.69$ for consumption), while the popular genres sit on the negative side (rap/hip-hop at $-1.26$ for consumption and indie rock at $-1.29$ for consumption). Whether we measure liking or listening, the same genres cluster together---the classic \emph{highbrow--popular hierarchy} that researchers have documented for decades \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,jæger2024from-a4b}. The hierarchy is strongly anchored in generation \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}, with older people tending toward the highbrow pole and younger people toward the popular pole, a result we discuss in Section~\ref{sec:social}. Status attributions, by contrast, barely move along this dimension (their genre positions range from $-0.23$ for rap/hip-hop to $+0.39$ for dance/club music). Dimension 1 is thus a \emph{highbrow--popular} axis.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-categories-d12} \caption{Category map of the MFA (dimensions 1--2). Colored labels mark the ``yes'' categories of each aspect; grey points are the corresponding ``no'' categories. On Dimension 1 the preference and consumption ``yes'' categories split highbrow (right) from popular (left); on Dimension 2 (volume) all of them sit on the positive side, the rarest engagements furthest from the origin. On Dimension 3 (engagement divide) the diaspora genres sit positive and the guitar-rock cluster sits negative. Evaluation ``yes'' categories barely spread on these three axes.}
\label{fig:categories1-2}
\end{figure}

Dimension 2 is a \emph{volume} axis, ordered by how much respondents engage at all. Every preference and consumption yes category sits on the positive side, and the rarer the engagement, the further out the category sits. Listening to folk ($+1.35$), bluegrass ($+1.31$), or big band ($+1.19$) places a respondent far along the axis, while listening to rap/hip-hop ($+0.05$) or heavy metal ($+0.03$) barely moves it, because those engagements are widespread. Liking follows the same rarity ordering (folk at $+0.84$, big band at $+0.80$, opera at $+0.78$ at the extremes). Evaluation yes categories follow rarity as well---granting status to blues/R\&B fans ($+0.59$), Latin/salsa fans ($+0.57$), or heavy metal fans ($+0.51$) is more distinctive than granting it to classical music fans ($+0.03$)---but they stay far closer to the origin than the engagement categories. Where respondents sit on this axis thus depends on the sheer volume of their engagement.

As Figure~\ref{fig:categories3-4} shows, dimension 3 separates the preference and consumption categories of non-highbrow genres by broad ``music world'' type rather than by prestige \citep{silver2022balancing-5a8}. The consumption yes categories for the Black, Latin, and Caribbean diaspora genres sit at the positive pole---reggae at $+0.95$, Latin/salsa at $+0.76$, rap/hip-hop at $+0.61$---while the guitar-rock cluster sits at the negative pole (heavy metal at $-0.91$, indie rock at $-0.76$). Liking mirrors the same contrast (rap/hip-hop at $+0.60$, Latin/salsa at $+0.51$, reggae at $+0.45$, against heavy metal at $-0.62$ and indie rock at $-0.53$), while evaluation is nearly silent (its yes categories span only $-0.33$ to $+0.17$). Where respondents sit on this dimension depends on which genres they engage with, and the dimension is strongly anchored in race and ethnicity (Section~\ref{sec:social}).

The vertical axis of the category map in Figure~\ref{fig:categories3-4} (Dimension 4) tells a different story. All twenty evaluation yes categories sit clustered on the positive side of the origin. The preference and consumption yes categories, by contrast, scatter around zero. On this dimension, the rarer the high-status attribution for a genre, the higher that genre sits (rap/hip-hop and Latin/salsa at $+1.94$, against $+0.02$ for classical music and $+0.00$ for opera)---popular genres receive high-status attributions from fewer respondents, making their fans appear as distinctive high-status recipients. This is the \emph{status-valuation} dimension, almost entirely an evaluation axis. A respondent's position here depends almost solely on how they distribute status recognition across genres' fans, independent of their liking or listening. Generous respondents---those who grant high status to fans of most genres---sit high on the vertical axis, while respondents who reserve high status for traditionally consecrated genres (like classical or opera) sit low.

\subsection{Relationships Between the Three Aspects}

Now that we have verified the aspects are distinct and seen what each dimension captures, we can ask two more foundational questions: Do all three aspects contribute equally to the global space, and do they dominate different dimensions?

\subsubsection{Participation: The Lg Coefficient}

Given that the aspects are partially independent, a second question arises: when we merge them into one compromise space, do all three actually show up, or does one get swallowed by the others? The Lg coefficient measures how much of each aspect's internal structure survives this merging process. It assesses the inner product of each aspect's configuration matrix with the combined MFA:

\begin{equation}
Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA}) = \frac{\mathrm{tr}(\mathbf{S}_h \mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{MFA}})}{N^2 \lambda_1(h)}.
\label{eq:lg}
\end{equation}

Here, $\mathbf{S}_h$ is the respondent-similarity matrix for aspect $h$ (defined in the previous section), $\mathbf{S}_{\mathrm{MFA}}$ is the combined respondent-similarity matrix from the global MFA, $N$ is the number of respondents, and $\lambda_1(h)$ is the first eigenvalue from the separate MCA of aspect $h$. In plain terms, $Lg(h, \mathrm{MFA})$ measures how much of aspect $h$'s internal structure---the pattern of which respondents are similar to which others based on that aspect---is preserved in the compromise space. If an aspect's structure is completely lost in the merge, $Lg$ is near zero; if it survives intact, $Lg$ is high. Because we deliberately weighted the aspects to give them equal voice, the $Lg$ is normalized so that perfect equal participation yields an $Lg$ of approximately $1$ for each aspect. 

Table~\ref{tab:groups} shows the estimated $Lg$ coefficients from the MFA analysis. Preference contributes 1.09, consumption 1.05, and evaluation 0.78. These values cluster near 1, indicating that all three aspects participate robustly in the global space. The slight shortfall for evaluation ($0.78$ rather than $1.0$) reflects its lower correlation with the liking and listening patterns that dominate the first three dimensions. Yet evaluation still contributes substantially, particularly through Dimension 4. This balanced participation signals that our weighting strategy succeeded: despite their very different distributions (evaluation is rarest), the three aspects speak equally to the overall structure.

\subsubsection{Aspect Contributions to Each Dimension}

Equal overall participation masks important asymmetries: the three aspects do not dominate equally on every dimension. Some dimensions are shaped primarily by liking or listening, while others belong to evaluation. The contribution of aspect $h$ to dimension $s$ is the sum of the squared coordinates of its twenty genre categories on that dimension, weighted and normalized by the dimension's overall variance:

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Ctr}(h,s) = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{J_h} w_j f_{js}^2}{\lambda_s}.
\label{eq:ctr}
\end{equation}

Here, $w_j$ is proportional to the rarity of affirmative responses for each genre, $f_{js}$ is the position of that genre's yes-answer category on dimension $s$, $J_h$ equals 20, and $\lambda_s$ is the dimension's eigenvalue. By construction, contributions sum to $100\%$ per dimension. 

Table~\ref{tab:groups} shows the resulting aspect contributions to each dimension. On Dimensions 1--3, the distribution of contributions is relatively flat, with consumption dominating Dimension 1 at 54.6\%, preference leading Dimension 2 at 52.3\%, and consumption again leading Dimension 3 at 56.3\%. Across the first three dimensions, evaluation contributes only 1.1\%, 4.2\%, and 3.1\% respectively. Preference and consumption pull in the same direction---the genre hierarchy and the intensity of engagement show up in both aspects' structures---even though the separate analyses order their internal axes differently. As we can see, Dimension 4 inverts this picture entirely. Evaluation overwhelms at 91.1\%, with preference and consumption relegated to minimal contributions of around 4.0\% each. What you like and listen to tells you almost nothing about how you distribute status attributions. Evaluation is genuinely its own story and its loose connection to preference and consumption is the primary source of complex tastes in these data.

\subsection{Measuring How Much Individual Tastes Come Apart}

So far we've asked about the space as a whole: How independent are the aspects? Do all three participate? Which aspect participates the most on which dimension? Now we flip back to the individual level, asking: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects agree or disagree?}

\subsubsection{Agreement and Disagreement Between Aspects}

To measure within-person disagreement, we proceed as follows. First, note that each person has \textit{three} separate coordinates on each Dimension---one from the separate MCA analyses of their preferences, one from the consumption analysis, plus a third one based on their evaluations---one per aspect. For Dimension 1, let us call these $F_{1,\text{p}}$, $F_{1,\text{c}}$, $F_{1,\text{e}}$. These three aspect-specific coordinates are called that person's three \emph{partial points} on the specified dimension of the compromise space. The partial points themselves are weighted by each aspect's balancing factor (the inverse of its first eigenvalue) so that they are expressed in the global MFA coordinate system. The global position is the average of these three partial points, which makes it the geometric center of the aspect-specific positions. Now all three of these points may be very close (and even coincide); alternatively, the three might not be very close. For instance, Person A might have all three coordinates at $+2$ (perfect agreement). Person B might have coordinates at $+3$, $+1$, and $-1$ (strong disagreement).

We measure this disagreement with a score called $W_s(i)$. This score answers the question: ``How much do person's $i$ three aspects disagree on dimension $s$?'' If all three dimension-specific scores are identical, $W_s(i) = 0$ (simple taste, complete agreement). If they're far apart, $W_s(i)$ is large (complex taste, substantial disagreement).

Mathematically, the following decomposition holds exactly:

\begin{equation}
\sum_{h=1}^{H} F_{sh}(i)^2 \;=\; H \cdot F_s(i)^2 \;+\;
\underbrace{\sum_{h=1}^{H} \left(F_{sh}(i) - F_s(i)\right)^2}_{W_s(i)},
\label{eq:decomp}
\end{equation}

Where $F_{sh}(i)$ is person $i$'s coordinate on dimension $s$ for aspect $h$ (the partial point), $F_s(i)$ is the person's global position on dimension $s$ (the average of the three aspect-specific coordinates), $W_s(i)$ is the disagreement score, and $H = 3$ the number of aspects being considered. The first term ($H \cdot F_s(i)^2$) measures how far from the center all three aspects place them together---their shared position. The second term ($W_s(i)$) measures the sum of squared deviations of each aspect's position from the mean, telling us how much the three aspects pull in different directions. Scaling up from individuals to the full sample: when we sum $W_s(i)$ across all respondents, $\sum_i W_s(i)$ gives the total disagreement variation on dimension $s$. Dividing this by the total variation across all coordinates, $\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2$, yields the proportion of the dimension's overall variation attributable to aspect disagreement. The remainder comes from variation in where respondents sit when all their aspects point the same direction---the shared consensus position.\footnote{Formally, the dimension-level disagreement share is $\sum_i W_s(i) / \sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2$. The denominator follows from Equation~\ref{eq:decomp} summed across all respondents, or $\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2 = \sum_i H \cdot F_s(i)^2 + \sum_i W_s(i)$, so the disagreement share plus the position share sum to one.}

To make this concrete, consider two respondents shown in Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}. One likes fifteen of the twenty genres---from jazz, classic rock/oldies, and country to top 40 and heavy metal---listens to nine of them, and credits the fans of eighteen genres with unambiguously high status (a somewhat ecumenical picture of the status of genres). The other likes fourteen genres, listens to thirteen, and grants high status to none---a stance of withholding evaluation despite high engagement. Both are heavy engagers, with global volume coordinates near $+3$, yet they differ sharply in how their three aspects align. On the \emph{highbrow--popular dimension} (left panel, horizontal axis), the first respondent's preference point sits well down the popular side ($-0.87$) while consumption and evaluation sit slightly on the highbrow side ($+0.20$ and $+0.22$), around a global point of $-0.45$. The second respondent's three aspect points are more dispersed: preference slightly below center ($-0.22$), consumption above it ($+1.11$), and evaluation slightly below ($-0.08$), averaging to a global point of $+0.82$. On the \emph{volume dimension} (right panel's horizontal axis), both respondents' three aspect points again cluster tightly (first: $+1.02$, $+1.14$, $+0.97$; second: $+1.13$, $+2.61$, $-0.23$), giving the first $W_2 = 0.13$---essentially zero disagreement---yet the second has $W_2 = 36.29$, placing them above the 99th percentile. The difference lies in the fourth dimension: the first respondent's evaluation point soars upward ($+4.81$) while preference and consumption cluster near zero ($-0.25$ and $-0.32$), creating $W_4 = 155.7$, while the second's three points all sit below center (ranging from $-0.88$ to $-0.16$), yielding minimal $W_4 = 2.8$. The same high engagement produces disagreement on different dimensions: respondent 362's complexity stems from evaluating generously while engaging selectively, while respondent 1881's stems from evaluating narrowly while engaging widely.

The rows show the respondents (top: one who grants high status to 18 of 20 genres; bottom: one who grants high status to none); the columns show different dimension pairs (left: highbrow--popular axis with status valuation; right: volume axis with status valuation). Colored points are the aspect-specific partial points (blue = preference, orange = consumption, green = evaluation); the black diamond is the respondent's global (compromise) position, their average. Solid segments, colored by aspect, connect each partial point to the compromise. The vertical spread (squared deviations along Dimension 4) shows status-valuation disagreement: the generous respondent has $W_4 = 155.7$ (93\% of their disagreement), while the withholding respondent has $W_4 = 2.8$ (22\%). Despite their opposite evaluation patterns, both respondents are heavy engagers who sit at nearly the same position on the volume dimension (right panels), yet their status-valuation disagreement differs by a factor of more than fifty.}
\label{fig:worked-example}
\end{figure}

\subsubsection{Pairwise Disagreements and Sources of Complexity}

But $W_s(i)$ hides an important detail: which two aspects are actually pulling apart? The score decomposes into three pairwise disagreements: between liking and listening, between liking and evaluations, and between listening and evaluations. Each pairwise distance measures how far apart two aspects place a person on this dimension. The three pairwise distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$, so we can ask: ``Which pair of aspects is responsible for most of the disagreement on this dimension for each individual?'' On some dimensions, the preference--evaluation and consumption--evaluation distances might dominate (because evaluations place people far from where liking and listening do), while on other dimensions these pairwise distances might be more evenly balanced.\footnote{The squared pairwise distance between aspects $h$ and $k$ is simply $(F_{sh}(i) - F_{sk}(i))^2$. The three distances sum exactly to $H \cdot W_s(i)$.}

Pairwise disagreements capture which aspects pull against each other, but they don't distinguish two very different mechanisms by which a person's taste becomes complex. A respondent might hold contradictory opinions of a single genre---liking it but not valuing it highly, for instance---or the same kind of disagreement might appear across multiple genres in a way that cancels out. Understanding these mechanisms matters because respondents with the same total $W_s(i)$ score can arrive there through entirely different patterns: some through intense within-genre contradictions, others through consistent contradiction that reinforces across the whole repertoire. We can decompose $W_s(i)$ to separate these two sources of disagreement as follows:

\begin{equation}
W_s(i) \;=\; \underbrace{\sum_{g=1}^{G} H^2 \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs}^2}_{\substack{\omega_s(i;g) \\ \text{genre-based}}} \;+\; \underbrace{2H^2 \sum_{g < g'} \sum_{h=1}^{H} d_{ighs} d_{ig'hs}}_{\substack{\gamma_s(i) \\ \text{coherence}}}
\label{eq:genre}
\end{equation}

The first term, $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$, captures the respondent's \emph{genre-based complex taste}: how much their three aspects contradict each other within specific individual genres. For each genre $g$, we measure deviations $d_{ighs} = c_{ihs} - \bar{c}_{ghs}$, where $c_{ihs}$ is respondent $i$'s partial point for aspect $h$ on dimension $s$, and $\bar{c}_{ghs}$ is the mean of all respondents' partial points for aspect $h$ on that genre (this is the genre's category score from the global MFA). For example, suppose genre $g$ has an average position of $0$ on dimension $s$ across all respondents. If this respondent's preference partial sits at $+2$, consumption at $-1$, and evaluation at $+3$, the three deviations are $+2$, $-1$, and $+3$; their squared sum makes $\omega_s(i;g)$ large for that genre. Summed across all twenty genres, $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$ captures total genre-based disagreement. This component is especially large when a respondent's three aspects contradict each other within specific genres---when a person likes a genre but doesn't value it (a guilty pleasure), or values it without listening to it (distant praise).

The second term, $\gamma_s(i)$, captures \emph{cross-genre coherence}: whether a respondent's per-genre deviations $d_{ighs}$ point in the same direction across different genres (reinforcing disagreement) or in opposite directions (cancelling disagreement). It measures whether the pattern of disagreement within a respondent is consistent or contradictory across genres. Formally, it sums the products of deviations for each pair of genres, within each aspect: if a respondent deviates positively for genre $g$ and negatively for genre $g'$ on the same aspect, the product is negative and reduces total disagreement. If the deviations both point the same way across genres, the product is positive and increases it. Positive $\gamma_s(i)$ means the respondent's per-genre disagreements reinforce each other across genres; negative $\gamma_s(i)$ means they cancel out.

Returning to our first respondent from the highbrow--popular example: the contrast comes on the \emph{status-valuation axis} (vertical, Dimension 4). Their preference and consumption points sit slightly on the withholding side of the origin ($-0.76$ and $-0.96$), while the evaluation point lies far out on the generous side ($+14.42$), since they grant high status to nearly every genre's fans. The global point is $+4.24$, and the disagreement dominates: $W_4 = (-0.76 - 4.24)^2 + (-0.96 - 4.24)^2 + (14.42 - 4.24)^2 = 155.7$, or 93\% of their variation on this dimension. Nearly everything that places this respondent on the status-valuation dimension is disagreement between aspects. The second respondent's evaluation point also sits on the withholding side ($-0.37$), with preference and consumption at the origin (since they have no opinions to report), around a global point of $-0.12$. Their $W_4 = 2.8$ (22\% of their variation) reflects mild geometry due to small coordinates throughout.

Despite their opposite evaluation patterns, both respondents are heavy engagers (similar positions on the volume dimension), yet their status-valuation disagreement differs by a factor of more than fifty. The first is complex on the status-valuation dimension alone; the second is not complex on any dimension.

To understand how genre-based and cross-genre coherence components combine, consider three respondents who illustrate the different mechanisms. Table~\ref{tab:respondent-typology} presents their profiles on the status-valuation dimension (Dimension 4), showing how the same total $W_4$ score can arise from vastly different sources. Respondent 522 (a low-disagreement case) likes five genres, listens to four, and grants high status to eleven, with all three aspect points clustering tightly around $F_4 = -0.36$; their $W_4 = 1.1$ consists almost entirely of genre-based disagreement (0.8) with minimal coherence ($\gamma_4 = +0.3$). By contrast, Respondent 362 (the high case shown in Figure~\ref{fig:worked-example}) displays the high-coherence profile: $W_4 = 155.7$ splits into only 11.2 genre-based and 144.4 coherence ($\gamma_4 = 144.4$), meaning 93\% of disagreement stems from per-genre contradictions that reinforce each other across all twenty genres---a consistent pattern where their evaluation aspect places them far from where their liking and listening place them, dimension after dimension. A hypothetical third respondent might hold high genre-based disagreement (say, $\omega_4 = 50$ from specific genres where they like but don't value, or vice versa) with negative $\gamma_4$ that cancels out, yielding a moderate or low total score despite holding many individual contradictions. These three patterns---tight clustering, reinforcing contradictions across the repertoire, and cancelling contradictions---show that respondents with identical configuration counts can have vastly different $W_s(i)$ scores, and vice versa.

\subsection{Measuring Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:antinomies}

Now we get to the core question: \emph{For each person, on each dimension, how much do their three aspects disagree?} We measure this with the score $W_s(i)$ (Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}), the dispersion of a person's three partial coordinates around their global position---the average location of those three aspect-specific coordinates. It's zero when all three aspects place them at the same location (simple taste) and grows as they place them further apart (complex taste).

What's surprising is how much complex tastes matter geometrically. On Dimension 1, the disagreement score accounts for 49\% of the total variation (inertia) on that dimension---meaning that 49\% of the variation comes from respondents' aspects disagreeing with each other, and 51\% comes from where respondents sit in the space when we average their three aspect positions (their global position).\footnote{These percentages are computed by summing the individual aspect-disagreement scores across all respondents, $\sum_i W_s(i)$, and dividing by the total inertia on that dimension: $\frac{\sum_i W_s(i)}{\sum_i \sum_h F_{sh}(i)^2}$, where $F_{sh}(i)$ is aspect $h$'s coordinate for respondent $i$ on dimension $s$. From Equation~\ref{eq:decomp}, the two components (aspect disagreement and global position) partition the total inertia exactly.} On Dimension 2, it's 55\% disagreement versus 45\% global position. On Dimension 3, it's 52\% disagreement versus 48\% global position. On Dimension 4, it's 66\% disagreement versus 34\% global position. This means aspect disagreement is roughly as important as where respondents sit when their aspects agree (their global position) in shaping the structure of the space. Complex tastes aren't a marginal phenomenon confined to a few unusual respondents. They're woven throughout the structure of the space.

But there's another way to measure complex tastes, one that counts instead of measuring. Ma's framework identifies eight configurations that people hold in individual genres: guilty pleasures, taste poses, distanced consumption, and so on (Appendix~\ref{app:configurations} defines them). You can tally how many of a person's 20 genres fall into complex configurations---a combinatorial count. How does this count relate to the geometric $W_s(i)$ score?

The correlations are interesting. Configuration count versus $W_s(i)$: on Dimension 1, $\rho = 0.17$; on Dimension 2, $\rho = 0.28$; on Dimension 3, $\rho = 0.18$; on Dimension 4, $\rho = -0.11$. Surprisingly weak, and the strongest correlation is with the volume dimension. Why? The configuration count is dimension-free---it just tallies how many genres you hold in contradictory configurations. The geometric score, by contrast, is dimension-specific: it measures how much disagreement matters on the axis you're looking at. They're answering different questions. Figure~\ref{fig:signatures} shows the geometric signatures of each configuration type. Each configuration occupies a distinct region of the space. But there's substantial variation within each configuration. Respondents with guilty pleasures, for instance, range widely on the status-valuation disagreement score---mean $W_4$ of $4.5$, but SD of $10.4$. Some people hold their guilty pleasure in intense contradiction across their three aspects; others barely do. The same configuration can manifest very differently depending on which genres hold it and how strongly the aspects disagree within those genres.\footnote{The supplementary Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} in the appendix visualizes the full range of within-configuration variation across all eight configurations and four dimensions.}

Heatmap shows Spearman correlations between configuration counts (per respondent, out of 20 genres) and MFA coordinates and complex-taste scores ($N = 2{,}259$), across four dimensions and three score types (global coordinates, aspect-disagreement, genre-based complex taste).}

\subsection{The Social Sources of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:social}

A fundamental question: \emph{Who has complex tastes?} We know taste positions are socially stratified---older people like highbrow music, younger people popular, and so forth \citep{bourdieu1984distinction,bennett2009culture-aef}. But are people who experience disagreement between their aspects concentrated in particular demographic groups, or scattered throughout?

Here's the surprising finding: complex tastes are scattered everywhere. When we model the disagreement scores $W_s(i)$ using demographics, we find that age, education, income, race, class, gender, parents' education, and region together explain only $4.4\%$ of the variation in $W_1$ (highbrow--popular), $3.6\%$ in $W_2$ (volume), $10.0\%$ in $W_3$ (engagement divide), and $1.9\%$ in $W_4$ (status valuation). 

Compare that to taste position, which is demographics-driven. Your global position on the genre hierarchy ($\eta^2$ ranging from 0.01 to 0.31) is predictable from your age and education. Researchers can forecast fairly accurately whether you lean highbrow or popular \citep{lizardo2015musical-8c6}. But aspect disagreement? Far more opaque. No demographic profile reliably predicts whether your liking, listening, and evaluations will line up or diverge. It's as if complex taste is woven throughout the population rather than concentrated in any particular social location.

The few effects that do appear show distinct patterns by dimension. On the highbrow--popular axis ($W_1$), disagreement declines with age, with the sharpest drop among respondents in their fifties (ages 50--59: $b = -1.65$, $p < .001$), while respondents in the South and West disagree less than those elsewhere (South: $b = -0.42$, $p = .030$; West: $b = -0.60$, $p < .001$). On the volume dimension ($W_2$), upper-class respondents show substantially more disagreement ($b = 4.54$, $p < .001$), as do those with college-educated parents ($b = 1.52$, $p < .001$). On the engagement-divide dimension ($W_3$), racial and ethnic differences are pronounced: Black respondents show more disagreement ($b = 1.61$, $p < .001$), as do those identifying with multiple races ($b = 1.41$, $p < .001$) and Hispanic respondents ($b = 0.52$, $p < .001$), while those 60 and older show substantially less disagreement ($b = -0.77$ and $-0.93$, both $p < .001$). On the status-valuation dimension ($W_4$), upper-class respondents show dramatically more disagreement ($b = 9.16$, $p < .001$), and those aged 30--49 show elevated disagreement (ages 30--39 and 40--49: $b = 2.42$ and $2.31$, both $p < .05$). The overall pattern is clear: different dimensions of disagreement are anchored by different demographics. The three aspects---liking, listening, evaluating---are weakly coupled overall, yet their specific patterns of disagreement vary by the dimension and the demographic group.

But this seemingly weak overall social patterning masks an important distinction. Recall that the disagreement score $W_s(i)$ decomposes into two components (Equation~\ref{eq:genre}): the \emph{genre-based} part $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$, which sums up how much a respondent's three aspects disagree within each of the twenty genres, and the \emph{cross-genre coherence} component $\gamma_s(i)$, which measures whether those per-genre disagreements reinforce or cancel each other across the full repertoire. To illustrate: a respondent might have high genre-based disagreement in rap (likes it, doesn't listen regularly, withholds status) and simultaneously in operatic music (doesn't like it, listens out of cultural obligation, grants status)---these work against each other in the total score when $\gamma_s(i)$ is negative, or together when it's positive. 

These two components of disagreement show strikingly different social patterns. The genre-based component is substantially more socially structured, with demographics explaining $22.2\%$, $7.9\%$, $20.1\%$, and $3.0\%$ of its variation across the four dimensions (compared to $4.4\%$, $3.6\%$, $10.0\%$, and $1.9\%$ for the total scores). Upper-class respondents show elevated genre-based disagreement on the volume dimension, and race/ethnicity strongly anchors the genre-based component on the engagement-divide dimension. The cross-genre coherence component $\gamma_s(i)$---whether per-genre disagreements align or cancel---is more weakly structured overall, with $R^2$ values around $3.5\%$, $3.5\%$, $7.1\%$, and $1.8\%$ across the four dimensions. Social position thus shapes which genres anchor the genre-based component of disagreement, while coherence follows a weaker patterning of its own. Section~\ref{sec:coherence} examines the coherence component directly.

\subsection{Which Genres Anchor Complex Tastes? Demographic Concentration}
\label{sec:genre-specificity}

In Section~\ref{sec:social}, we found that demographics explain little of the total disagreement ($W_s$), yet the genre-based component $\sum_g \omega_s(i;g)$ shows substantially stronger social structure. This raises a natural question: \emph{In which specific genres does demographic position shape disagreement?} The answer reveals that demographic concentration in complex tastes varies sharply by both genre and dimension, and that social location channels disagreement into culturally meaningful objects.

Figures~\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d4} show which genres concentrate these demographic effects most sharply. The eight genres displayed are those where patterns are most pronounced: rap/hip-hop, indie rock, and dance/club for the age gradient on the highbrow--popular dimension; big band at its older pole; classical music, opera, and musicals for education and class effects; and Latin/salsa for the largest race-indicator effect. Every cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable and that genre's genre-based component $\omega_s(i;g)$: own education and subjective class as four category indicators each, age, parental education, and gender as measured, and race and ethnicity as category indicators. Census region shows no genre-specific concentration anywhere in the taste space (no correlation reaches $|r| = 0.10$), so it is omitted. Blue cells indicate positive correlations (higher disagreement in that demographic category); red cells indicate negative correlations. 

Which socio-demographic groups experience disagreement relative to which genres? We organize findings by the four dimensions.

\emph{On the highbrow--popular dimension}, age creates the sharpest patterns. Younger respondents hold more genre-based disagreement in the popular genres---rap/hip-hop ($r = -0.44$), indie rock ($-0.36$), heavy metal ($-0.27$), and dance/club ($-0.25$)---while older respondents show more in folk ($0.22$) and big band ($0.18$). Race and ethnicity matter here as well. Hispanic respondents show elevated disagreement in Latin/salsa ($r = 0.44$), and White respondents show the mirror image in Latin/salsa ($-0.34$), rap/hip-hop ($-0.27$), and reggae ($-0.22$). Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$), blues ($0.23$), and rap/hip-hop ($0.20$). Postgraduate respondents show somewhat more disagreement in opera ($r = 0.17$).

\emph{On the volume dimension}, the same race and age contrasts appear in somewhat weaker form (Hispanic respondents in Latin/salsa, $r = 0.34$, against $-0.30$ for White respondents; older respondents in big band, $0.19$, and younger in indie rock, $-0.21$), alongside an education gradient in the consecrated genres. Postgraduate respondents show elevated genre-based disagreement in opera ($r = 0.17$) and musicals ($0.15$), and respondents with college-educated parents show it in opera, classical music, and musicals ($r = 0.12$ each). Upper-class respondents show elevated disagreement in opera ($r = 0.15$), though their other correlations are small.

\emph{On the engagement-divide dimension}, the age and race patterns of the first dimension recur at nearly the same strength (rap/hip-hop $r = -0.44$ and indie rock $-0.34$ for age; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White; blues $0.26$ and rap/hip-hop $0.20$ for Black respondents). The overlap reflects the two dimensions' shared basis in liking and listening. The engagement-divide dimension nevertheless adds its own reading, since the disagreement it registers concentrates in the contrast between the diaspora genres and the guitar-rock cluster, the axis most strongly anchored in race and ethnicity (Section~\ref{sec:social}).

\emph{On the status-valuation dimension}, the associations are weak throughout, consistent with demographics explaining little of the variation in that component ($R^2 = 3.0\%$). The largest correlations are postgraduate respondents in opera ($r = 0.18$) and older respondents in big band ($0.16$); no other correlation reaches $|r| = 0.15$.

The genre-based component thus becomes a window onto how demographic position works. It shapes not just whether people sit on the highbrow or popular side of the genre hierarchy (taste position), but \emph{where} and \emph{how} their aspects come apart (taste structure). Social location doesn't uniformly make people's aspects disagree more or less; instead, it directs that disagreement toward specific cultural objects. Demographics channel complex tastes through particular genres that carry social meaning and group identity.

The eight-genre matrices above foreground the largest demographic effects; the supplementary appendix (Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}) extends these to all twenty genres and all sixteen demographic indicators, showing where the patterns hold and where they fade. The full matrices reveal that the demographic shaping of disagreement is genuinely genre-specific: each demographic group's complex tastes concentrate in a distinct subset of the repertoire, and few correlations exceed $|r| = 0.15$ outside the genres highlighted above. This pattern validates the interpretive claim: demographics shape which genres people find disagreeable, not whether they experience disagreement.

\subsection{The Social Patterning of Cross-Genre Coherence}
\label{sec:coherence}

The genre-based component is socially patterned: age, race, education, and class channel disagreement into different genres. But what about the coherence component---the reinforcing or cancelling of per-genre disagreements across the full repertoire? 

We tested this with the same demographic variables and methods. The pattern is striking in its near-absence: bivariate associations are tiny. Gender shows nothing anywhere. Only one association reaches even $\eta^2 = 0.05$---race/ethnicity on the engagement-divide dimension at $0.049$, which is also the dimension where race most strongly shapes the genres themselves. The total disagreement scores show the same near-null pattern: their largest bivariate association is also race on the engagement-divide dimension ($\eta^2 = 0.064$). Coherence, like aspect disagreement itself, is not the signature of any particular demographic group.

The joint regression models tell the same story with a little more structure. Demographics explain $3.5\%$ of the variation in $\gamma_1$ (highbrow--popular), $3.5\%$ in $\gamma_2$ (volume), $7.1\%$ in $\gamma_3$ (engagement divide), and $1.8\%$ in $\gamma_4$ (status)---weaker than the genre-based component's $22.2\%$, $7.9\%$, $20.1\%$, and $3.0\%$. The effects that do appear concentrate on $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_3$. On the highbrow--popular dimension, coherence declines across the middle age cohorts ($b = -1.12$ at ages 50--59, $p < .001$), though the oldest cohort no longer differs from the youngest, and postgraduate respondents show somewhat more coherence ($b = 0.61$, $p < .05$). On the engagement-divide dimension, race dominates: Black respondents show substantially higher coherence ($b = 1.43$, $p < .001$), as do respondents identifying with more than one race ($b = 0.99$, $p < .01$), while the Midwest and West show slightly lower coherence ($b = -0.40$ and $-0.55$, both $p < .05$). The volume dimension's few effects---coherence higher among respondents with college-educated parents ($b = 1.33$, $p < .001$) and among upper-class respondents---belong to the class story taken up below. The status-valuation dimension shows the least structure of all ($R^2 = 1.8\%$). Gender and household income show nothing reliable on any dimension.

Because Equation~\ref{eq:genre} is an identity, and the coherence models use the same sample and predictors as the models for the total scores, every coefficient in Section~\ref{sec:social} splits exactly into a genre-based and a coherent part. This attribution sharpens the reading of the class and family-background results. The upper-class premium on $W_2$ (volume: $b = 4.54$) is almost entirely coherence ($b = 4.09$), with only a small genre-based part ($b = 0.45$). Upper-class respondents' disagreement on the volume dimension, in other words, does not take the form of contradictions lodged in particular genres. It takes the form of a repertoire-wide alignment, with the same aspect displaced in the same direction across genre after genre, so that the per-genre deviations reinforce one another instead of cancelling. This is the empirical counterpart of the toy contrast in the analytic strategy---the same total disagreement can be assembled from a single genre held in intense contradiction or from twenty genres tilted the same way, and social position helps decide which assembly a person's disagreement takes.

Coherence is not always reinforcing. Substantial proportions of respondents show negative coherence, meaning their per-genre disagreements partially cancel and their total disagreement is smaller than the sum of its genre-level parts: about a third on the highbrow--popular dimension ($33\%$), a quarter on the volume dimension ($25\%$), and more than half on the engagement-divide dimension ($52\%$). One caveat concerns the status-valuation dimension. Evaluation is the only aspect that varies there, so a respondent who grants high status to many genres displaces their evaluation point in the same direction for every genre at once. For such respondents, much of what $\gamma_4$ records is this uniform displacement rather than configural contradiction, which is why $\gamma_4$ correlates with the magnitude of the global position ($r = 0.78$) more strongly than any other coherence score. Where coherence has social structure, then, it reflects these repertoire-wide orientations rather than localized contradiction. The genre-anchored form of complex taste---the kind whose social geography the previous section mapped---is the genre-based component's contribution.

\subsection{The Duality: Genres as Targets of Complex Tastes}
\label{sec:duality}

Complex tastes have a dual structure. We've traced them from the individual perspective: \emph{who} has complex tastes, and \emph{what} aspects disagree. But genres are targets too. Which genres attract complex tastes? The answer: some genres generate much simpler responses than others.\footnote{At the genre level, we measure the proportion of respondents with simple tastes: those whose three aspects all agree (either all yes---like, listen, grant status---or all no). The complement is the proportion with complex tastes in that genre (any mismatch across aspects).}

Heavy metal, Latin/salsa, and bluegrass produce largely simple tastes: $70\%$, $67\%$, and $65\%$ of respondents respond consistently across all three aspects. You either like them and listen and value them, or you don't. Classical and opera are different. Only $33\%$ and $24\%$ of respondents respond simply to these genres. The rest hold them in contradiction: they might like classical music but rarely listen to it, or they listen out of cultural obligation while withholding judgments about the fans, or they think the music lacks status yet listen regularly. These prestige genres splinter audiences into complex configurations.

To answer this, we need a different analysis. The first MFA treated respondents as the units being analyzed and genres as variables. Now we flip that: rows become genres and columns become respondent-responses (each respondent's yes/no on liking, listening, and evaluation for each genre). We re-run the MFA with genres as units. This is not simply a rearrangement of the original solution; it is a fundamentally different analysis that asks new questions. In the original analysis, genres appeared only as variables; we could locate them through the composition of their audiences---the average profile of people who affirm them. But we cannot compute aspect-level agreement from the respondent analysis alone. Specifically, we cannot ask whether genres that are \emph{liked by many} are also \emph{listened to by many}---that is, whether the liking and listening audiences for each genre overlap. We also cannot see whether different aspects place individual genres in different positions. Both questions require treating genres as the units of analysis and respondents as the indicators.

Technically, this flip changes the analysis fundamentally. Because MFA weights each block inversely to its separate analysis's strength in the first dimension, and transposing reshuffles which variables define the blocks, the balancing weights change: the transposed separate analyses yield different first eigenvalues ($\lambda_1' = 0.153/0.161/0.419$ for preference/consumption/evaluation respondent-indicators, versus the original $0.155/0.127/0.194$ for genre-indicators). The transposed dimensions are thus optimized for spreading genres apart, not respondents. The key statistics we want---RV coefficients comparing aspects at the genre level, and aspect-specific partial points showing where different respondent-groups place each genre---do not exist in the respondent-level fit.\footnote{The transposed MFA was implemented by direct application of the algorithm in \citet{pages2014mfa} and validated by reproducing the respondent-level analysis: eigenvalues, global and partial coordinates, RV coefficients, and group contributions are numerically consistent.}

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-genre-map-d12} \caption{Genre map from the transposed MFA (dimensions 1--2). Black points: genre compromise positions; colored points: aspect partial points (segments connect each genre's compromise to its aspect-specific positions).}
\label{fig:genre-map-d12}
\end{figure}

Here's what's striking: From the genre perspective, the aspects \emph{agree} far more strongly. The RV coefficients jump to $0.92$ (preference and consumption nearly identical), $0.53$ (preference and evaluation), and $0.48$ (consumption and evaluation)---much higher than the individual-level $0.35$, $0.01$, and $0.02$. At the genre level, people who like a genre tend to listen to it and grant its fans high status. Genres that recruit likers recruit listeners too.

But this doesn't contradict what we found at the individual level---it's the ecological fallacy in reverse. The liking audience and the listening audience overlap substantially for each genre. But the \emph{same individuals} don't always inhabit both groups. The person who likes opera but doesn't listen is in the liking audience; the person who listens but doesn't like is in the listening audience. Separately, they agree. Together, at the aggregate genre level, they agree. But at the individual level, people split apart. Complex tastes aren't something genres do; they're something individuals experience. Which individuals respond simply and which complexly varies person by person.

\centering \caption{Genre target profiles: percentage of respondents holding each genre in each of Ma's configurations ($N = 2{,}259$).}
\label{tab:genre-profile}

The transposed space is itself strongly structured ($\lambda_1 = 2.25$, $14.8\%$ of the inertia; $\lambda_2 = 1.93$, $12.8\%$; $\lambda_3 = 1.25$, $8.2\%$; $\lambda_4 = 1.12$, $7.4\%$), with the first four dimensions accounting for $43.2\%$ of the total variation. The first two dimensions are shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}, and the fourth dimension is shown in Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d14}. 

The first dimension opposes genres whose typical relation is status without engagement---classical ($-3.6$), opera ($-3.0$), and musicals ($-2.1$), with distant-praise rates correlating at $\rho = -0.82$ and taste-pose rates at $\rho = -0.58$---against genres most often held in the guilty pleasure ($\rho = +0.75$)\footnote{The correlation coefficients ($\rho$) reported throughout this section are Spearman rank correlations between each genre's coordinate on the transposed dimension and the genre-level prevalence (proportion of respondents, across all 2,259) who hold that genre in each of Ma's eight configuration types. For example, $\rho = +0.75$ for guilty pleasure on Dimension 1 means that genres with high positive coordinates on that dimension tend to have high prevalence of guilty pleasure configurations, while genres with negative coordinates tend to have low prevalence of that configuration.} and distanced consumption ($+0.80$) configurations. These last include top 40 ($+2.0$), rap/hip-hop ($+1.8$), classic rock/oldies ($+1.3$), and contemporary rock ($+1.3$)---familiar genres most often held with engaged disagreement. This dimension, in plain terms, measures the \emph{engagement--detachment} contrast at the genre level: on the negative side sit prestige genres whose audiences are defined partly by abstention from engagement (the listener who values classical music highly but rarely listens), while the positive side includes genres where respondents' disagreement arises from active engagement despite reservations about status (the guilty-pleasure listener who loves the genre but withholds attributing high status to the genre's audience). In effect, this dimension answers the question: Does a genre recruit audiences through engagement or through distant admiration?

The second dimension is a \emph{configuration axis}: genres are ordered by the complex-taste profiles they attract (Table~\ref{tab:genre-profile}; Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}). At the positive pole sit the genres respondents actively hold---in simple positive taste ($\rho = +0.77$), as taste poses ($+0.55$), as guilty pleasures ($+0.44$), or as justified abstentions ($+0.44$)---led by classic rock/oldies ($+3.7$), mood/easy listening ($+2.0$), country ($+1.8$), and top 40/pop ($+1.3$). At the negative pole sit genres whose dominant relation is simple non-taste ($\rho = -0.73$): rap/hip-hop ($-1.7$), reggae ($-1.5$), latin/Spanish/salsa ($-1.3$), and heavy metal ($-1.3$)---together with opera ($-1.2$), whose characteristic relation to its audience is instead dominated by distant praise (with $58.9\%$ of respondents holding it in that configuration). The duality is asymmetric in exactly the way complex-taste theory anticipates: the prototypical guilty-pleasure genres are among the least credited with high status (evaluation rates of $8$--$14\%$ for classic rock/oldies, country, and top 40), and the prototypical distant-praise genre is the least consumed ($8.5\%$ for opera).

The partial points reveal how audiences for the same genre diverge by aspect. Like in our original MFA analysis focused on individuals, in the transposed MFA, each genre has three partial coordinates per dimension: one for the preference-audience (respondents who like it), one for the consumption-audience (respondents who listen), and one for the evaluation-audience (respondents who grant it high status). When these three points cluster together, a genre recruits the same people across all three aspects---likers and listeners and status-granters occupy the same region. When they spread far apart, a genre's audiences are segmented: the people who like it are positioned differently from those who listen to it or who value its fans highly. The configuration axis (Dimension 2 of Figure~\ref{fig:genre-map-d12}) shows this segmentation most starkly: certain genres (rap, reggae, metal) have their liking and listening audiences positioned on the negative pole but their evaluation audience positioned on the positive pole---meaning that people who grant these genres high status are a demographically and culturally distinct population from the people who actually like or listen to them. 

More broadly, three patterns emerge: opera stands alone with extreme segmentation across all dimensions---its status-granting audience is a separate population at every level of analysis. At the opposite end, classic rock and country show the strongest engagement-without-status pattern, where listeners are numerous but status-granters are scarce. Most other genres recruit relatively unified audiences where the same people like, listen, and evaluate, or where segmentation concentrates on a single dimension rather than cutting across multiple ways of relating to the music.

The fourth dimension captures how genres attract audiences whose status valuations diverge from their engagement patterns. The evaluation partial points of consecrated genres sit displaced toward positive values relative to their preference and consumption partial points (classical: $+2.3$ for evaluation against $+1.0$ for preference and $+0.9$ for consumption; opera: $+2.3$ against $-0.0$ and $+0.1$), while country shows the reverse displacement (evaluation $-0.8$ against $-3.1$ and $-4.1$). In substance, this dimension measures the \emph{status--engagement separation} at the genre level: prestige genres sit high not because their audiences like or listen more, but because status attributions extend to genres people rarely engage with, creating a population of evaluators distinct from the liking and listening audiences. Popular genres sit low, meaning their status-granting audiences are smaller or nonexistent relative to their liking audiences. This is the genre-level complement to the individual-level status-valuation dimension (Dimension 4 at the individual level): whereas respondents on that axis range from those who grant status to few genres to those who grant it to many, this genre-level dimension reveals which genres suffer the sharpest separation between who engages with them and who credits their fans with high status.

\section{Discussion}

This paper has pursued a geometric approach to measuring complex tastes---the misalignments between preference, consumption, and evaluation in cultural fields. The results support three core findings about musical taste in contemporary America.

\emph{First, the three aspects are empirically independent.} Preference and consumption correlate moderately (RV = 0.35), but evaluation is nearly orthogonal to both (RV = 0.01). This independence is the geometric signature of the complex-taste concept. If all three were measuring the same underlying thing, we could ignore two of them. But they don't. What you like, what you listen to, and what you praise are three separable judgments that follow different logics.

\emph{Second, the shared structure is primarily two-dimensional.} The first dimension is the classical highbrow--popular hierarchy. The second is volume: how many genres someone likes and listens to. Both dimensions are visible across all three aspects, reflecting shared cultural structures that shape how people organize musical taste. Evaluations are largely silent on these dimensions, appearing only modestly on the first and second, but dominating a distinct fourth dimension.

\emph{Third, complex tastes are ubiquitous.} The disagreement scores ($W_s$) account for $49\%$, $55\%$, $52\%$, and $66\%$ of variation on the four dimensions. Combinatorially, the average respondent holds $10.2$ of $20$ genres in complex configurations. Only 12 respondents (of 2,259) hold no complex configuration at all. This is not a marginal phenomenon. Complex tastes are woven throughout the taste landscape.

A surprising finding follows: complex tastes are not concentrated in any social group. Where respondents sit (whether they prefer highbrow or popular genres) is strongly predicted by age, education, and class. But how much their three aspects disagree is nearly unpredictable from demographics. The dispersion that makes a person's taste complex is orthogonal to the social positions that sort people by consumption patterns. This fits the individual-level theory. The independence of the aspects at the population level generates disagreement at the individual level whenever people don't occupy all three positions simultaneously.

Finally, the duality reveals something crucial: from the genre perspective, the aspects agree. Liking, listening, and evaluation audiences overlap substantially. But because individuals don't equally participate in all three audiences, complex tastes emerge. A person may be a genuine opera enthusiast (likes, listens, praises) or a genuinely uninterested person (none of the above) or any combination. The eight configurations are not rare types; they're how ordinary people relate to culture when three incompletely correlated judgment systems structure their engagement.

Future work might explore whether these patterns generalize to other cultural fields---visual art, film, fashion---or whether music has distinctive properties. The geometric approach makes possible precise measurement of the degree to which cultural judgment is unified or fragmented. The results here suggest it's fundamentally fragmented.

\section{Within-Configuration Variation in Disagreement Scores}
\label{app:config-variation}

Respondents classified into the same configuration type show substantial variation in their aspect-disagreement scores across all four dimensions. Figure~\ref{fig:config-variation} displays the mean and standard deviation of $W_s$ for each configuration, revealing that the overlap in disagreement levels both within and across configuration types explains why the correlation between the geometric and combinatorial measures is weak. This variation arises because the same configuration can manifest across different numbers of genres and with different internal structures: a respondent with one guilty pleasure genre will have very different W scores than one with many such genres, even though both respondents hold the same configuration type. The disagreement associated with a particular configuration depends not just on its presence, but on how spread out across the genre space it becomes.

\begin{figure}[htbp]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{fig-config-variation} \caption{Aspect-disagreement scores by configuration type. Bars show the mean $W_s$ for each of Ma's eight configurations on each of the four dimensions; error bars show $\pm 1$ SD. The substantial overlap both within and across configuration types illustrates why configuration counts and geometric disagreement scores are only weakly correlated.}
\label{fig:config-variation}
\end{figure}

\section{The Combinatorial Measure: Ma's Eight Configurations}
\label{app:configurations}

The geometric measure locates complex tastes continuously in the common space. As a discrete complement, each genre--respondent pair can be classified into one of Ma's eight configurations from the binary triple of orientations (preference, consumption, evaluation): the simple taste $(+++)$, the simple non-taste $(---)$, and the six complex configurations.

Complex tastes are the statistical norm, not the exception \citep{ma2026deep-fb3}. Figure~\ref{fig:configurations} reports the mean number of genres held in each configuration: the average respondent holds $10.2$ of the $20$ genres in a complex configuration, and only $12$ of $2{,}259$ respondents hold no complex configuration at all. The most frequent complex configuration is the \emph{justified abstention} ($3.3$ genres on average), followed by the \emph{guilty pleasure} ($3.2$) and \emph{distant praise} ($2.2$): respondents routinely like genres whose fans they don't credit with high status, grant high status to genres they neither like nor consume, and like-and-consume genres whose fans they don't think of as high status. The taste pose ($1.0$) and the rare variants---distanced consumption ($0.4$) and the pre-acquired taste ($0.1$)---are comparatively infrequent, while the simple non-taste ($8.9$) is the single largest configuration.

\section{Genre-Specific Disagreement Across All Twenty Genres}
\label{app:omega-genres}

Figures~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4} extend the genre-by-demographic matrices of Figures~\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d4} to all twenty genres, one figure per dimension. Each cell reports the Pearson correlation between a demographic variable (columns) and the genre-based component $\omega_s(i;g)$ of the genre named in the row. All sixteen demographic variables are shown---the four own-education categories (high school or less, some college, bachelor's, postgraduate), parents' education, the four subjective-class identities (lower, working, middle, upper), age, gender, and the White, Black, Hispanic, Asian, and Multirace/Other category indicators. The encoding is as in Figures~\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d1}--\ref{fig:omega-demographics-d4}; blue cells are positive, red cells negative, and every value is printed.

The matrices confirm how localized the demographic patterning is. On the highbrow--popular dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d1}) the age gradient dominates the popular block (rap/hip-hop $-0.44$, indie rock $-0.36$, heavy metal $-0.27$), the race indicators peak in Latin/salsa (Hispanic respondents $0.44$, White $-0.34$), and Black respondents show elevated disagreement in gospel ($0.25$) and blues ($0.23$). On the volume dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d2}) the education contrasts appear (postgraduate respondents $0.17$ for opera and $0.15$ for musicals, parents' education $0.12$ for opera, classical music, and musicals) alongside the race contrasts in the diaspora genres (Hispanic respondents $0.34$ for Latin/salsa, Black respondents $0.20$ for gospel and $0.18$ for reggae). On the engagement-divide dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d3}) the first dimension's age and race patterns recur at nearly full strength (rap/hip-hop $-0.44$; Latin/salsa $0.43$ for Hispanic respondents against $-0.34$ for White). On the status-valuation dimension (Figure~\ref{fig:omega-genres-d4}) the associations are weak throughout; the largest is postgraduate respondents in opera ($0.18$).
